text: Our analysis from lesson eleven had a hard-coded filter: amount over ten thousand, thirty days overdue. But what if someone wants to rerun it next week with a different threshold, without asking you to edit it? That's filters versus prompts.

A filter is a fixed condition baked in when the analysis is built. Every time it runs, for any user, that threshold applies. Filters are right when the condition genuinely shouldn't change, like "payment status equals unpaid" for an open-invoices analysis.

A prompt asks the person running the analysis to supply a value before results render, a dropdown, a date range, a text box. The same analysis design gets reused, but each viewer can get a different slice. A Business Unit prompt lets each regional AP lead see only their own region from one shared analysis, instead of building ten near-identical copies.

On the view side: Table shows plain rows, closest to a raw export. Pivot Table aggregates facts across dimensions on rows and columns, with subtotals, dragging a dimension from rows to columns reshapes the whole view instantly. Graph renders the same data as bar, line, or pie, for a quick visual read instead of exact figures.

An analysis isn't limited to one view, a detail table for drill-down plus a graph for the summary, both from the same column selection. Up next, lesson thirteen: combining several analyses into a dashboard.
